all_quotes.quote: Our sample is overall clearly biased towards barred galaxies, since as many as 19 out of 24 galaxies (79%) are barred according to (cite: 2021A&A...656A.133Q).

For some galaxies, the offsets at certain radii are exceedingly large because at that point the spiral is nearly tangent to the circular bins where we perform the measurements (very low pitch angle); this is the case for NGC 1300, for example.
Our offset measurements rely on galactocentric radial bins, which implicitly assume circular trajectories for gas and stars.

This means that if there is a systematic displacement between gas and star formation along the orbit, that distance will be underestimated by our circular bins, especially for more open spirals (large pitch angle) with strong stellar arm/interarm contrasts.

We find that perturbing the orientation parameters within their error bars has a typical impact on the offsets and correlation coefficients of at most a few multiples of 10%, and importantly, it does not significantly wash out any radial trends.
Another methodological detail that might be questionable is the choice of H$\alpha$ to trace recent star formation, as this optical tracer is known to suffer from severe extinction.

However, dust extinction could be stronger in ‘upstream’ locations compared to ‘downstream’ regions (due to higher gas column densities), and it could also be stronger near the centres of the galaxies.
Another related problem could be associated with changing star formation timescales (cite: 2024ARA&A..62..369S), which could make the radial behaviour more erratic.
It is worth noting that even in the framework of quasi-stationary density wave theory, the mean measured offset for a given galaxy will depend on the field of view.
The limited field of view also affects our ability to test whether offsets indeed become negative after a certain radius, as we commented on in Sect. [5.3](#Sec:single_OmegaP).
